This is a classic presentation of metastatic spinal cord compression. It is usually due to cancer of the prostate, breast or lung that has spread into the vertebrae. Compression of the whole of the canal causes a loss of pain and temperature sensation on the lower half of the body (below the level of compression), as well as reduced or absent light touch and proprioception. It also causes variable degrees of weakness below the level of compression. The motor function is often better than the sensory function. In this case, the MRC is grade 5 - which means that there is movement against gravity but not against resistance. The pain and temperature sensation on the upper half of the body is unaffected because the spinothalamic tract lies close to the middle of the spinal cord. The sensory signs are lost above the level of compression because it takes 2-3 seconds for sensory information to travel up the spinal cord. The patient may have urinary incontinence. It is important to distinguish between metastatic and extradural spinal cord compression, as the latter requires emergency surgery. Vitamin A (or more specifically, its precursor, beta-carotene) is required to produce a substance called 'Rhodopsin' which allows your eyes to adjust to low levels of light when you enter a darkened room. If you have a vitamin A deficiency then this substance will not be produced meaning that it takes much longer for your eyes to get used to lower levels of light. This is known as night blindness. It is also needed in the formation of melanin which gives colour to the skin and hair. A lack of vitamin A causes the cornea to become very thin and translucent resulting in 'xerophthalmia'. It also causes hyperplasia of sebaceous glands in the scalp and face leading to 'follicular hyperkeratosis'. This excess keratin produced can be removed by combing or brushing but it is usually permanent and may lead to scarring and pitting of the skin. Digoxin is used to treat heart failure by increasing the force of contraction and reducing the rate of heart rate. It does this by blocking Na+/K+ ATPase in the cardiomyocyte which flips the movement of ions across the NCX causing an increase in intracellular calcium. This results in stronger contractions and slower heart rates.  The NCX channel is found on the sarcolemma of cardiac myocytes and is responsible for Ca2+ uptake during systole and release during diastole. The Na+/K+-ATPase pump moves sodium out of the cell and potassium into the cell. Both of these are involved in maintaining the electrochemical gradients for calcium. Aldosterone's only role is to increase sodium reabsorption and therefore increase blood pressure. It does this by upregulating Na/K pumps in the epithelial cells of the collecting duct and distal convoluted tubule. This has the effect of increasing water absorption and decreasing potassium levels in the blood. ADH is released from the posterior pituitary gland and acts on the collecting duct to increase aquaporin channel expression and H+ATPase activity. The increased H+ATPase activity increases the production of H+ which combines with buffers such as bicarbonate to form carbonic acid. Carbonic acid dissociates into carbon dioxide and water which are then able to be excreted from the body via the collecting duct into the ureter and finally into the bladder and urethra. The increase in aquaporins allows more water to pass through the cell membrane, down its concentration gradient and into the collecting duct, increasing urine output. The increase in H+ATPase also decreases the permeability of the cell membrane to potassium so that it can be removed from the bloodstream and concentrated in the urine. This results in increased urine osmolarity and decreased blood osmolarity.  Source - Case 12 lecture on Kidney physiology and pathophysiology.
